messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Input: Piezoelectric transducer (current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ || $C_p$ || $R_{\text{leak}}$).
    *   Output: Storage capacitor at node "out" powering load $R_L$.
    *   Requirements:
        *   $V_{\text{avg}} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{\text{max}} \le 3.6\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{\text{pp}} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $t_{\text{up}} \le 0.4\text{s}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $dV \le 0.02\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
    *   Piezo Params: $C_p \approx 25\text{nF}$, $f \approx 100\text{Hz}$, $I_p$ varies ($30-100\mu\text{A}$).
    *   Open-circuit voltage amplitude: $V_{oc} = \frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p} \approx \frac{50\mu\text{A}}{2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 3.18\text{V}$.

    *   FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) failed:
        *   S2 (heavy load): $V_{\text{avg}}$ too low ($1.76\text{V}$), $t_{\text{up}}$ missing.
        *   S3 (light load, strong exc): $V_{\text{max}}$ too high ($5.72\text{V}$), $V_{\text{pp}}$ too high ($84\text{mV}$), $dV$ failed.
        *   S4 (weak excitation): $V_{\text{avg}}$ too low ($1.51\text{V}$), $t_{\text{up}}$ missing, $dV$ failed.
        *   S5 (low frequency): $dV$ failed.

    *   Key issues:
        1.  **Voltage Drop:** The FBR uses 2 diode drops ($\sim 0.5\text{V}$ total). For low excitation (S4), the available voltage is already low, and the diode drops push it below $1.8\text{V}$.
        2.  **Overvoltage:** Under light load/strong excitation (S3), the output voltage climbs too high (exceeding $3.6\text{V}$).
        3.  **Efficiency:** Passive rectification is inefficient for low-voltage sources.

    *   **SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):** This is the gold standard for piezo energy harvesting. It uses an inductor and a switch to invert the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively increasing the harvested energy and the voltage delivered to the rectifier.
    *   **Active Rectification (Synchronous Rectification):** Using switches instead of diodes to eliminate the $V_f$ drop. However, the available `SYNC` controller and `S` switches are limited (max 4 switches, 2 SYNCs).
    *   **Zener Clamp:** To prevent $V_{\text{max}} > 3.6\text{V}$, a DZ33 Zener diode can be used on the `out` node.

    *   *Approach 1: SSHI-like (Parallel SSHI).*
        Use an inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ to flip the charge on $C_p$ at the peaks. Then rectify into the storage capacitor.
        Wait, the `SYNC` controller allows closing switches at extrema.
        A simple SSHI implementation: Inductor $L$ in series with a switch $S$, connected across the piezo.
        Wait, the standard SSHI requires a rectifier *after* the flip.

    *   *Approach 2: Synchronous Rectification (Active Bridge).*
        Instead of diodes, use switches. But we only have 4 switches and 2 SYNCs.
        A full bridge needs 4 switches. A half-bridge (voltage doubler/inverter) might work.

    *   *Approach 3: Half-Wave Synchronous Rectification with Inductor (Boost-like).*
        Using an inductor to store energy during part of the cycle and then dumping it into `out`.

    *   *Approach 4: FBR + Zener + Optimized Capacitor.*
        The FBR failed mainly on $V_{\text{avg}}$ for S2/S4 and $V_{\text{max}}$ for S3.
        If we use SSHI, we increase the efficiency and the voltage.

    *   **Proposal 1: SSHI-modified Full Bridge.**
        Circuit:
        1.  Piezo terminals `pzp`, `pzn`.
        2.  Inductor $L_1$ and switch $S_1$ (controlled by `SYNC G1`) in parallel with the piezo to flip charge.
        3.  Standard FBR (4x DSCH) to move charge from the piezo to `out`.
        4.  Zener diode DZ33 from `out` to `0` to clamp $V_{\text{max}}$.
        5.  Storage capacitor $C_{\text{out}}$ on `out`.

        *Wait, let's check the switch constraints.* Max 4 switches. Max 2 SYNCs.
        The flip: $S_1$ closes at both peaks.
        The bridge: 4 diodes.
        The clamp: 1 zener.
        Total components: $L_1, S_1, G_1, D_1, D_2, D_3, D_4, D_{\text{zener}}, C_{\text{out}}$. (9 components).
        This should increase the voltage available to the diodes, helping S2 and S4. The Zener fixes S3.

    *   **Proposal 2: Synchronous Rectification (Half-bridge/Charge Pump).**
        Since $V_{oc}$ is low, maybe a synchronous switch rectifier is better.
        Let's try a "Synchronous Switch" circuit that dumps charge into `out`.
        Wait, the simplest way to avoid diode drops is using the switches themselves to rectify.
        But SYNC only triggers at extrema.
        If we use `edges: "pos"`, $S_1$ closes at the positive peak. If we use `edges: "neg"`, $S_2$ closes at the negative peak.
        But to get charge to `out`, we need a path.

        Let's refine Proposal 1 (SSHI + FBR + Zener).
        SSHI (Parallel): $L$ and $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
        $L$ is connected between `pzp` and a node `n1`. $S$ is between `n1` and `pzn`.
        When $S$ closes, the energy in $C_p$ oscillates through $L$.
        But we still need a rectifier to get it to `out`.

    *   **Proposal 3: A Simplified Synchronous Converter (Charge Pump).**
        Use $L$ to boost the voltage.
        $L$ from `pzp` to `n1`. $S_1$ from `n1` to `0`.
        When $S_1$ is closed (at the peak), $L$ charges.
        When $S_1$ opens, $L$ discharges through a diode into `out`.
        This is basically a boost converter synchronized to the piezo.
        With `edges: "both"`, we can do this twice per period.

    *   **Refining Proposal 1: SSHI + FBR + Zener.**
        Piezo: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        FBR:
        D1: `pzp` -> `out`
        D2: `pzn` -> `out` (Wait, FBR is usually: D1 `pzp`->`out`, D2 `pzn`->`out` is not possible. It's D1 `pzp`->`out`, D2 `0`->`pzn`, D3 `pzn`->`out`, D4 `0`->`pzp`? No. Standard FBR: `pzp` -> `out` via D1, `pzn` -> `out` via D3, `0` -> `pzp` via D2, `0` -> `pzn` via D4. No, that's not it.)
        Standard FBR connectivity:
        D1: `pzp` to `out`
        D2: `pzn` to `out`
        D3: `0` to `pzp`
        D4: `0` to `pzn`
        *Wait, that's not a bridge.*
        Correct FBR:
        D1: `pzp` to `n_top`
        D2: `pzn` to `n_top`
        D3: `0` to `n_bot`... no.
        Let's use the bridge provided in the Reference:
        `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`
        Wait, looking at the Reference design description:
        `full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`
        Let's check this:
        D1: `pzp` -> `out`
        D2: `pzn` -> `out`
        D3: `0` -> `pzp`
        D4: `0` -> `pzn`
        This is not a standard bridge. A standard bridge is:
        D1: `pzp` -> `out`
        D2: `0` -> `pzp` (wrong)
        Actually:
        D1: `pzp` -> `out`
        D2: `pzn` -> `out`
        D3: `0` -> `pzp`
        D4: `0` -> `pzn`
        Wait, if `pzp` is positive, D1 conducts. If `pzn` is positive, D2 conducts.
        But the other side? If `pzp` is positive, `pzn` is negative. D4 would conduct (`0` -> `pzn`).
        So:
        D1: `pzp` -> `out`
        D4: `0` -> `pzn`
        (Current path: `0` -> D4 -> `pzn` -> piezo -> `pzp` -> D1 -> `out`)
        And for the other half cycle:
        D2: `pzn` -> `out`
        D3: `0` -> `pzp`
        (Current path: `0` -> D3 -> `pzp` -> piezo -> `pzn` -> D2 -> `out`)
        This is a full bridge.

        Now, let's add the SSHI part:
        L1: `pzp` to `n1`
        S1: `n1` to `pzn`
        G1: `SYNC` controller.
        This flips the charge.

        And the Zener:
        DZ1: `0` to `out` (Cathode on `out`)

    *   **Comparing the Proposals:**
        1.  **SSHI + FBR + Zener:** High efficiency, clamps voltage, should solve S2/S4 (efficiency) and S3 (overvoltage).
        2.  **Synchronous Boost (Active):** $L$ and $S$ to boost, then diode to `out`.
            $L$ from `pzp` to `n1`, $S$ from `n1` to `0`, D from `n1` to `out`.
            This only harvests one polarity. To get both, we need another set or a symmetric structure.
        3.  **Half-Bridge Synchronous Rectifier:**
            $S_1$ from `pzp` to `out`, $S_2$ from `pzn` to `out`.
            Wait, `SYNC` only closes for `ton`. This is a switched-capacitor style.

    Let's stick with SSHI + FBR + Zener as the primary candidate. It's a proven topology for this.

    *   L1: $10\text{mH}$ (starting point)
    *   Cout: $2.2\mu\text{F}$
    *   ton: $\pi \sqrt{L C_p} = \pi \sqrt{10\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 15.7\mu\text{s}$.
    *   S1: `edges: "both"`, `phase: 0` (triggers at voltage extrema).

    *Wait, the `SYNC` controller triggers at current zero crossings, which are voltage extrema.*

    Let's double-check the FBR again.
    D1: `pzp`, `out`
    D2: `pzn`, `out`
    D3: `0`, `pzp`
    D4: `0`, `pzn`
    Check:
    Cycle 1: `pzp` high, `pzn` low. Path: `0` -> D4 -> `pzn` -> piezo -> `pzp` -> D1 -> `out`. (Correct)
    Cycle 2: `pzn` high, `pzp` low. Path: `0` -> D3 -> `pzp` -> piezo -> `pzn` -> D2 -> `out`. (Correct)

    Wait, the reference design used FBR and failed S2, S3, S4.
    S2/S4 failed $V_{\text{avg}}$ (too low). SSHI increases the voltage.
    S3 failed $V_{\text{max}}$ (too high). Zener clamps it.

    Is there any other way?
    What if we use a synchronous rectifier instead of diodes in the bridge?
    We only have 4 switches.
    S1: `pzp` -> `out`
    S2: `0` -> `pzn`
    S3: `pzn` -> `out`
    S4: `0` -> `pzp`
    But the `SYNC` controller is designed for the L-Cp inversion (short pulses), not for rectification (half-period pulses).
    The `ton` is limited to $1\text{ms}$, whereas a half-period is $5\text{ms}$ (at $100\text{Hz}$).
    So synchronous rectification is not possible with the provided `SYNC` controller.

    Therefore, the SSHI + FBR + Zener is the most viable path.

    *   D1: `pzp` -> `out` (DSCH)
    *   D2: `pzn` -> `out` (DSCH)
    *   D3: `0` -> `pzp` (DSCH)
    *   D4: `0` -> `pzn` (DSCH)
    *   DZ1: `0` -> `out` (DZ33)
    *   L1: `pzp` -> `n1`
    *   S1: `n1` -> `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
    *   G1: `SYNC`, `ton=15.7u`, `edges="both"`, `phase=0`
    *   Cout: `out` -> `0`

    Wait, the $V_{oc}$ is $3.2\text{V}$. The Zener is $3.3\text{V}$. The diodes drop $0.25\text{V} \times 2 = 0.5\text{V}$.
    So the max voltage without SSHI is $3.2 - 0.5 = 2.7\text{V}$? No, the piezo charges the capacitor. The peak voltage will be higher because the capacitor integrates the current.
    In S3, $V_{\text{max}}$ was $5.72\text{V}$. The DZ33 will clamp this to $\sim 3.3\text{V}$.

    Wait, if I use SSHI, the voltage across the piezo is flipped, which essentially increases the voltage delivered to the bridge.
    The inversion happens at the peaks.

    One detail: The inductor $L$ and switch $S$ should be in parallel with the piezo.
    `L1`: `pzp` -> `n1`
    `S1`: `n1` -> `pzn`
    This is correct.

    Wait, let's consider a second proposal just in case.
    What if the FBR is too lossy?
    Could we use a half-bridge?
    `D1`: `pzp` -> `out`
    `D2`: `0` -> `pzp` (no)
    Actually, if we use a center-tapped transformer... but we don't have one.
    What about a charge pump?
    $S_1$ from `pzp` to `n1`, $S_2$ from `n1` to `out`.
    Again, `ton` is too short for this.

    So, let's stick with SSHI. Let's try two variations of the SSHI.
    Variation 1: SSHI + FBR + Zener.
    Variation 2: SSHI + FBR (without Zener, maybe the evolution strategy finds a way, but S3 will likely fail). Actually, let's try SSHI + FBR + Zener as the main and maybe a "half-wave" SSHI?
    No, "both" edges is better.

    Let's refine the components for Proposal 1.
    L1: $10\text{mH}$
    Cout: $2.2\mu\text{F}$
    S1: `ton=15.7u`
    G1: `edges="both"`, `phase=0`
    FBR: DSCH
    DZ1: DZ33

    Wait, is $15.7\mu\text{s}$ a good `ton`?
    $t = \pi \sqrt{L C_p} = \pi \sqrt{10\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} = 15.7\mu\text{s}$.
    The evolution strategy will optimize this, but it's a good start.

    *   S1: Nom.
    *   S2: Heavy load (150k). FBR failed $V_{\text{avg}}$. SSHI should boost efficiency.
    *   S3: Strong exc, light load (2200k). FBR failed $V_{\text{max}}$ and $V_{\text{pp}}$. Zener should clamp $V_{\text{max}}$.
    *   S4: Weak exc (30uA), light load (1000k). FBR failed $V_{\text{avg}}$. SSHI should help.
    *   S5: Low freq (80Hz). FBR failed $dV$. A larger Cout or better efficiency should help.
    *   S6: Hot, $C_p$ +20%.

    One potential issue: The SSHI switch `S1` and inductor `L1` create a resonant circuit.
    If $S_1$ closes at the peak, it flips the voltage.
    $V_{pzp}$ goes from $V_{peak}$ to $-V_{peak}$.
    This increases the voltage delivered to the diodes.

    Wait, if $V_{peak}$ is already $3.2\text{V}$, and we flip it, the diodes will see $3.2\text{V}$.
    But the FBR's problem in S4 was that the peak voltage was too low to overcome the diode drops effectively?
    $V_{oc}$ in S4: $I_p = 30\mu\text{A} \Rightarrow V_{oc} = \frac{30\mu\text{A}}{2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 1.9\text{V}$.
    With a $0.5\text{V}$ drop, you only get $1.4\text{V}$, which is below $1.8\text{V}$.
    SSHI increases the effective $V_{oc}$ to the rectifier. Specifically, it allows the capacitor $C_p$ to be discharged more completely.

    Wait, I just noticed that for the FBR in the reference, $V_{\text{max}}$ was $5.72\text{V}$ in S3.
    If $V_{oc}$ is $3.2\text{V}$ (nominal) or $6.4\text{V}$ (S3), the FBR can easily reach $5.7\text{V}$.
    So the DZ33 Zener is definitely needed.

    Let's double check the total component count:
    L1 (1), S1 (1), G1 (1), D1-D4 (4), DZ1 (1), Cout (1) = 9 components. Well within the 16 limit.

    One more thing: `S1` switch control.
    `"ctrl": "G1"`
    `"G1": { "ton": ..., "phase": ..., "edges": ... }`
    This matches the requirements.

    Let's consider if there's any other topology.
    What if we use a "Voltage Doubler" (Greinacher circuit)?
    It uses 2 diodes and 2 capacitors.
    C1 (storage), D1, C2 (transfer), D2.
    But this only harvests one polarity.
    A full-bridge is generally better for piezo unless $V_{oc}$ is very high.

    Final check on FBR connectivity again:
    - D1: `pzp` -> `out`
    - D2: `pzn` -> `out`
    - D3: `0` -> `pzp`
    - D4: `0` -> `pzn`
    Wait, let's re-trace:
    Cycle 1: `pzp` = +V, `pzn` = -V.
    Path: `0` -> D4 -> `pzn` -> piezo -> `pzp` -> D1 -> `out`.
    Current flows: $0 \to \text{D4} \to \text{pzn} \to \text{pzp} \to \text{D1} \to \text{out}$.
    Cycle 2: `pzp` = -V, `pzn` = +V.
    Path: `0` -> D3 -> `pzp` -> piezo -> `pzn` -> D2 -> `out`.
    Current flows: $0 \to \text{D3} \to \text{pzp} \to \text{pzn} \to \text{D2} \to \text{out}$.
    Yes, this is a perfect full-wave rectifier.
